text: Taeo pressed his thumb into his palm, searching for the pulse. Nothing. With Nib on the other side of the gate, the link had gone silent.
Inside, Nib stood on a cliffside gallery under a lavender sky, a sheer drop beyond the old stone supports. Far ahead, white stone streaked the cliff.
Outside, six minutes had passed. Haein fiddled with the radios, Sejin ate her kimbap, and Taeo stood at the safety tape, clutching his log.
He drifted past the tape without noticing. Haein hooked a finger through his vest and pulled him back without even turning around.
The knock was due at forty minutes, Sejin reminded him, not six. Taeo had called waiting hard before. Now he was learning what it meant.
Inside, Nib insisted on carrying the long tripod case. His determination outlasted his balance. The wooden mule managed its load considerably better.
So Nib handed it over and assigned the jobs. 'You carry. I look.' Minho suggested he start looking.
Nib scouted ahead, calling out loose grit over the radio. He pressed his hand to the cliff. Outside, Taeo's palm stayed silent.
Twenty minutes. Another train rumbled past, the fourth, and Taeo flinched again. Sejin told him to sit. He was fine, he insisted.
Haein asked why he didn't go in with Nib. He couldn't, Taeo said. Nothing more.
Her father had gone first on every job. Now Minho did. Haein built things so she could help from outside.
Twenty-seven minutes in, Nib stopped near the white outcrop. Above them, grit trickled from a hairline crack.
He pointed out the damaged strut. Minho couldn't see the crack. Watch the grit, Nib said. Then Minho saw it.
The outcrop was their last survey station. Minho braced the strut with a steel prop and sent them through one at a time. The mule stayed behind.
Nib went first, alone, under the cracked support, toward the white stone.
Outside, Haein counted down the last ten seconds. Forty minutes.
Taeo knocked twice, carefully, just as agreed. They waited. Nothing came back.
If Nib was fine, Taeo decided, he was never speaking to him again.
Then the gate shuddered and spat out grit. Another train? Sejin was already reaching for her medical kit. That sound had come from inside.
Taeo hammered two more knocks into the steel and split a knuckle. Haein stared at the gate over her stopwatch, waiting for her brother.
Then, from inside, three knocks. Three meant coming. Taeo made a sound somewhere between a laugh and a sob.
Nib stepped out covered in stone dust, his fist closed around something small.
The moment he was back, amber flooded Taeo's palm. He could feel him again.
Nib held up a chalk-white pebble. The same stone as the white patch beside his wall.
Taeo's legs gave out, and he sat down hard on the edge of the walkway. Nib looked down at him. 'You look worse than me.'
They had been too far away to hear the knocks, Nib explained, and Minho hadn't made it past the cracked strut yet. Once Minho was safe, Nib ran back.
Sejin checked Taeo with her penlight. He hadn't even been inside, he protested. 'No. You were out here.'
She handed Nib water. He passed it straight to Taeo. 'You first.' Taeo finally laughed.
Minho and the mule came out dusty but unhurt. The strut had collapsed behind Minho and blocked the bend. But the survey was done.
Minho blamed Nib for a new white hair. 'You're welcome,' Nib said, perfectly straight-faced.
Knocks crossed the gate, Haein noted, but didn't carry far. Maybe a cable could carry the radio signal. Minho's first question was the price.
That night, Nib counted his sixty thousand won for forty-three minutes inside. Taeo explained day rates. Nib decided he liked them.
He placed the white pebble on his drawing, filling the blank outline beside the path below his watch post.
Did that mean home was close? Nib would only say what he knew. The stone matched.
A late news alert cut in. A porter was missing after a Dokgo Contracting job in Guro.
The missing worker was in his sixties. Behind a cordon, other porters watched violet gate light beyond the hoarding. This wasn't a mule, Taeo told Nib. This was a human porter.
A young woman clutched her hard hat, crying at the chained entrance. Dokgo's statement: the man had left voluntarily.
